sections.h2: Who gets the house when there is no will
sections.html:
Chapter 732 of the Florida Statutes sets the order. Spouse and descendants come first, then parents, then siblings, then more distant kin. Who actually takes depends on who survives, and a house that counts as homestead follows extra rules.

"Intestate" means the owner died without a valid will, or with a will that leaves the property out. In that case the Probate Code names the people who take title. A sale still needs someone with court-given authority to sign the deed, so the order of heirs mostly tells you who receives the proceeds and who must agree.

The answer turns on the children. Section 732.102 gives the spouse the whole intestate estate in some families and half in others.

  • No surviving descendants of the decedent: the spouse takes everything.
  • Every descendant of the decedent is also the spouse's descendant, and the spouse has no others: the spouse takes everything.
  • At least one descendant of the decedent is not the spouse's: the spouse takes one-half.
  • All the decedent's descendants are shared with the spouse, but the spouse also has descendants from outside the marriage: the spouse takes one-half.

Blended families are where disputes begin. If the spouse has children from an earlier relationship, the share drops to half even when every child of the decedent is also the spouse's child.

sections.h2: Who inherits next, or when there is no spouse
sections.html:
Section 732.103 sets a ladder. A step applies only when every step above it is empty. The whole estate, or whatever the spouse does not take, moves down this list.

  1. The decedent's descendants.
  2. The father and mother equally, or the survivor of them.
  3. Brothers and sisters, with the descendants of any who died.
  4. Grandparents, then aunts, uncles and their descendants, split between the paternal and maternal sides, half to each.
  5. Kindred of the last deceased spouse, as if that spouse had survived and then died without a will.

If one side of the family has no living kin, the estate goes to the other side.

sections.h2: The family home with a spouse and children
sections.html:
By default the spouse gets a life estate and the children get the remainder. Section 732.401 covers homestead property the owner did not leave by a valid devise.

The remainder is vested in the descendants alive at death, divided per stirpes. A life tenant can live in the house but cannot deliver full title to a buyer alone, so these homes often stall at sale time.

The spouse can choose a different split: an undivided one-half interest as a tenant in common, with the other half going to the descendants. The choice must come within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime. It cannot be undone, and it is made by recording a sworn notice of election with the clerk in the county where the home sits. If the spouse is incapacitated, an attorney in fact or guardian needs court approval first, and that petition must also be filed within the 6 months.

Property held as tenants by the entireties, or with a co-owner under a survivorship arrangement, falls outside this section.

sections.h2: How heirs sell an inherited house
sections.html:
Heirs open a probate estate, have a personal representative appointed, and sell through that representative. Small estates may use a shorter court procedure.

Summary administration under section 735.201 fits an estate whose non-exempt assets are $150,000 or less, or one where the owner died over two years ago. Where only exempt property and a limited amount of other personal property remain, section 735.301 lets a court authorize transfer without full administration. Houses seldom qualify, so ask the probate clerk or a probate attorney.

Creditors get a limited window. Under section 733.702 a claim is barred unless filed by the later of two dates: 3 months after the notice to creditors is first published, or 30 days after a creditor entitled to direct service receives it. Buyers and title companies look for that clock, and for a recorded order or letters of administration, before they close.

sections.h2: Tax and deed costs when heirs sell
sections.html:
Three costs show up on a sale: deed tax, clerk recording charges and property tax changes. State estate tax ended with federal changes for deaths after 2004, and since July 2023 personal representatives skip the DR-312 and DR-313 filings.

A deed from the estate to a buyer is a taxable document. Section 201.02 sets the rate at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and every party to the document is liable, whoever agrees to pay. No specific exemption exists for estate planning transfers, so even a quitclaim among siblings can be taxed. A deed from the personal representative under a probated will is not taxable.

The clerk's recording charges are set in section 28.24, and the clerk's office can quote the total for your deed's page count.

On property tax, a title transfer sends the assessment back to just value on the following January 1, though certain transfers at death are carved out. Heirs who rent the home lose homestead. The appraiser's office can confirm how the parcel is treated.

sections.h2: Documents the title company will ask for
sections.html:
Expect requests for the death certificate, the court letters or summary administration order, and a copy of the will if there is one. If a spouse made the six-month election, bring the recorded notice. If the owner left a spouse and no election was recorded, bring proof of that so the title insurer knows what the spouse holds.

Every heir who takes an interest has to be identified. When the family tree is simple, an affidavit may be enough, but a blended family usually means more paper. Start early, because tracking down a missing signature is what delays most inherited sales.

A cash buyer can skip the lender's appraisal and underwriting, though the title company still needs all of these documents before it will insure the deed.

faqs.q: Does a surviving spouse always inherit the whole house in Florida?
faqs.a: No. The spouse takes everything only when the decedent had no descendants or all descendants are shared with the spouse. If one descendant is not the spouse's, section 732.102 gives the spouse one-half. For a homestead with a spouse and descendants, section 732.401 usually gives the spouse a life estate in place of full title.

faqs.q: Can a surviving spouse choose half of the homestead instead of a life estate?
faqs.a: Yes. The spouse may elect an undivided one-half share, held in common with the descendants, within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime. The election cannot be undone and is recorded as a sworn notice in the county where the home sits.

faqs.q: Who inherits if there is no spouse and no children?
faqs.a: The parents share equally, or the survivor takes it all. If neither lives, the estate passes to siblings and the descendants of deceased siblings, then to grandparent and aunt and uncle lines split between the paternal and maternal sides.

faqs.q: Is summary administration available for a house?
faqs.a: Sometimes, when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less or the owner died more than 2 years ago (section 735.201). Whether your house qualifies depends on the estate's value and the court's order, so check with the probate clerk or an attorney.

faqs.q: Is there a Florida estate tax on inherited homes?
faqs.a: No. Florida has no estate tax for deaths after 2004, and personal representatives no longer file Form DR-312 or DR-313. Documentary stamp tax can still apply to deeds, but a deed from a personal representative under a probated will is not taxed.
